canonical_statement: The study developed and evaluated GatorOnco, an agentic large language model specialized for colorectal cancer treatment planning.
GatorOnco domain adaptation combined continued pre-training, model merging, two-stage post-training, and agent-based reinforcement learning.
The biomedical pre-training corpus contained 282 billion tokens.
The Methods report 166 billion tokens of UF Health clinical narratives collected from 2011 to 2025 across more than 60 million encounters and 126 departments.
Clinical notes associated with the colorectal cancer cohort were excluded from the pre-training corpus using IRB-specific patient identifiers to reduce data leakage.
The curated colorectal cancer dataset contained 395 unique UF Health cases.
The final 395-case cohort was partitioned into 276 training, 40 validation, and 79 held-out test cases using stratified sampling.
The Results section also describes 316 cases as the model-development training set and 79 cases as the test set.
Eligible CRC cohort members were adults aged 18 years or older.
Eligible CRC cohort members required a confirmed primary colorectal cancer diagnosis based on ICD diagnosis codes and tumor registry records.

inclusion_criteria: Confirmed primary CRC diagnosis via ICD codes and tumor registry records

canonical_statement: Three board-certified UF Health oncologists manually reviewed candidate notes and annotated treatment options, treatment plan sections, and supporting clinical evidence.
Each case was independently annotated by at least two oncologists, with disagreements adjudicated by consensus and unresolved disagreements decided by a senior oncologist.
Oncologists categorized therapies into surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and palliative care.
The retrieval corpus used NCCN colon cancer guideline version 4.2025 and rectal cancer guideline version 3.2025.
NCCN guideline PDFs were parsed into narrative recommendations and stepwise rules, then segmented into semantically coherent chunks of 256 plus-or-minus 50 tokens aligned to paragraph boundaries.
Guideline chunks were embedded with E5-large-v2 and indexed in a FAISS vector database.
Guideline chunks were annotated with cancer type, stage group, metastatic status, metastatic site, and MSI/MMR status; initial annotation was assisted by ChatGPT-5 and reviewed by two oncologists.

The post-training corpus included about 23.5 thousand general clinical reasoning examples, a CRC-specific reasoning dataset derived from 276 training cases, and guideline factual question-answer pairs.
The Results section reports 6.8 thousand guideline-derived question-answer pairs, 23.5 thousand case-report-style clinical reasoning examples, and 316 CRC development cases used for fine-tuning.

CRC-specific reasoning trajectories were distilled with GPT-oss-120B from raw notes or oncologist-reviewed patient profiles paired with expert-verified plans, and oncologists reviewed and corrected the distilled trajectories.
Historical treatment plans were reviewed and updated by oncologists as needed for concordance with contemporary NCCN standards before reasoning distillation.
GatorOnco started from Meta-Llama-3.1-8B, underwent continual pre-training, and was merged with Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using mergekit-evo to retain instruction-following ability.
The merged model underwent supervised fine-tuning on more than 20,000 medical reasoning question-answer pairs.
Agentic RAG training used Group Relative Policy Optimization, with the model dynamically retrieving indexed NCCN guideline context during reasoning.
The hierarchical reward gave regimen-level reward only when the high-level treatment modality was correctly inferred, implementing a safety-first hard constraint.
During inference, GatorOnco could generate structured search actions that paused generation, retrieved top-ranked NCCN chunks, appended them to context, and then resumed reasoning.
GatorOnco achieved a macro-F1 score of 0.924 for single-therapy determination.
GatorOnco achieved an F1 score of 0.979 for chemotherapy determination.
GatorOnco achieved an F1 score of 0.964 for surgery determination.
GatorOnco achieved an F1 score of 0.933 for radiotherapy determination.
GatorOnco achieved an F1 score of 0.889 for targeted therapy determination.
GatorOnco achieved an F1 score of 0.857 for palliative care determination.
GatorOnco achieved an F1 score of 0.913 for determining multiple therapies that could be considered.
GatorOnco exactly matched the oncologist-annotated multiple-therapy set in 73 of 79 test cases (92.4%).

The blinded human evaluation mixed GatorOnco plans, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct plans, and oncologist-authored ground-truth plans for 79 test cases, producing 237 plans reviewed independently by five UF Health oncologists.

Human evaluators rated correctness, currency, safety, readability, and completeness on a 5-point Likert scale; analyses used a linear mixed-effects model plus dimension-specific Aligned Rank Transform tests with Holm-Bonferroni-adjusted Wilcoxon comparisons.
Krippendorff alpha for completeness ratings was 0.849.

canonical_statement: The study was limited to a single disease domain and a single institution, and note structures, documentation conventions, and data quality may differ across health systems.
Model performance fluctuated with prompting structure despite harmonized study inputs, and prompt-agnostic robustness remains unresolved.
Expert-level performance on 79 held-out cases does not establish readiness for deployment in cancer care.
The authors state that real-world deployment would require fail-safe mechanisms, uncertainty quantification, deferral policies for low confidence, and integration with clinical workflows.
The authors argue that machine-readable clinical guidelines with explicit schemas and change logs would better support concurrency-aware healthcare AI systems.
UF Health IDR clinical notes are not publicly available because of patient privacy; the authors state that the 79 de-identified test cases will be released through GitHub.
The manuscript reports that GatorOnco code is available in a public GitHub repository and identifies supporting repositories for pre-training, model merging, and agentic RL/inference.
The study reports support from PCORI, ARPA-H, NIH institutes, and the UF Clinical and Translational Science Institute.
